sections.text:

evening. Localized flooding due to heavy rainfall is possible, in

sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Issued at 247 PM EDT Wed Sep 23 2026

Currently, a shortwave is moving through the area overhead with an 
upstream jet approaching from the west and inverted surface 
troughing. This has put the region in the left-exit region of the 
jet, leading to large-scale lift. When combined with PWAT values of 
1.3 to 1.4 inches, this has and will continue to provide support for 
showers and storms during the afternoon and evening. Morning 
convection and clouds has limited heating and destabilization in 
some areas, but up to 1,000 J/kg of MLCAPE is expected. With 
freezing levels of 14,000 feet or higher and recent rain for some, 
efficient warm rain processes continue to emphasize localized flash 
flooding as the main concern. Some gusty winds are possible but not 
to the same degree as flooding. CAMs differ on how much coverage 
lasts overnight, but intensity will be lessened as instability is 
lost. By Thursday, troughing will have moved off to our east, 
leading to less upper support. Still, inverted surface troughing and 
lingering moisture will keep at least low-end chances for rain in 
the area. During this time, a low in the Atlantic will be deepening 
as upper troughing moves overhead. 

By Friday, the low in the Atlantic will deepen into a Nor'easter as 
it moves along the New England coast. This will lead to broad 
northwesterly flow across the region, pulling down cooler and drier 
air associated with high pressure to the north. Dry and more fall-
like weather can be expected with widespread highs in the 70s 
expected through the weekend. Radiational cooling, especially Friday 
night, will allow lows to drop into the 50s and upper 40s in the 
northeast. Another warming trend is expected early next week as 
heights rise and another surface low develops in the Great Plains, 
leading to a southerly shift in winds. 

&&

sections.title: AVIATION
sections.text:
(00Z TAFS)
Issued at 748 PM EDT Wed Sep 23 2026

Slow moving showers and storms will continue for the central
valley near TYS for the next 2 or so hours, and then should taper.
Unclear if TRI will see any TS, so kept it at shower. CHA has a
lingering shower nearby but should be done very soon. Overnight
low stratus will provide for widespread MVFR at best conditions,
with slow lifting of the stratus layer tomorrow. A few light
showers between 10z and 15z are possible, but not expecting
thunder. A return to VFR is possible before the end of the TAF
period, but uncertainty remains over when the stratus layer
scatters or lifts.

enso.title: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory
paragraphs: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory Synopsis: El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. El Niño strengthened further over the past month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +3.0°C in the eastern equatorial Pacific [Fig. 1] . Except for the Niño-4 index, which decreased to +0.1°C in August, values in the other Niño indices increased, reaching +1.8°C in Niño-3.4, +2.5°C in Niño-3, and +3.4°C in Niño-1+2 [Fig. 2] . The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) remained steady during August [Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline [Fig. 4] . Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth. Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies extended from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific. Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia [Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices remained negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño. The CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year [Figs. 6

-8] . During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ). With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies). In summary, El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. This discussion is a consolidated effort of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA's National Weather Service, and their funded institutions. md.areas: parts of southwestern North Dakota and adjacent portions of southeastern Montana and northwestern South Dakota
md.summary: Isolated strong thunderstorm development posing at least a risk for severe hail appears increasingly probable by 4-6 PM MDT. This may be maintained for a couple of hours late this afternoon into evening. Although this is still not anticipated to require a severe weather watch, trends will be monitored.
md.discussion: Stronger boundary-layer warming and deeper mixing has become focused near a weak surface low across the southeastern Montana/western Dakotas border vicinity, with some north-northeastward development still possible through late afternoon. Near the interface of this environment, and a narrow corridor of better low-level moisture return to the north/east, it appears that boundary-layer destabilization may maximize around the Dickinson, ND vicinity by 22-00Z. Aided by lift associated with a corresponding focused area of stronger low-level warm advection, as low-amplitude mid-level troughing continues to overspread the region, it appears that thunderstorms will initiate as remaining inhibition erodes. Near and just to the northwest of a strong southwesterly mid/upper jet (including speeds on the order of 40-70 kt in the 500-700 mb layer), updraft inflow of boundary-layer air characterized by CAPE up to 1000+ J/kg may support an evolving supercell structure. As this tends to propagate eastward, or east-southeastward, it may pose primarily a risk for severe hail, with perhaps some potential for locally damaging surface gusts and/or a brief tornado, for at least a couple of hours late this afternoon into evening.
